newsitem.title: USA: Stock drop not seen as big factor in budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Stock drop not seen as big factor in budget talks.

text.p: The recent stock market downturn will not affect budget talks because the underlying economy is still growing and that should help deficit reduction efforts, analysts said Thursday.

"The budget talks are going to be much more related to the Washington phenomenon, to politics, than they are to anything going on in the financial markets," Stan Collender, managing director at Burson-Marsteller, said.
"This is a change from two years ago when the Federal Reserve and Wall Street had a fairly big impact, but right now it's just not there," he said.
The Dow Jones industrial average has fallen about 600 points since its record close of 7,085.16 on March 11. On Thursday, the Dow closed down 39.66 points at 6,477.35.

"The stock market is declining partly because of bonds, and bond rates are rising because of a growing economy, so at the moment the projection for corporate profits is going up not down," Collender said.
Stock market declines would only affect the budget deficit if they signalled impending recession, which is not the current scenario, analysts said.
"To me the stock market is a reflection of things rather than a cause of things," a Democrat congressional aide said.

"Certainly if the financial markets believe that there's going to be a recession now ... well of course that would have profound implications for the budget talks ... make them harder," the aide said.

"But if it's just the stock market is declining because a speculative bubble has been pricked and that the real economy just keeps tooling along pretty much the way it has, then I don't see why that should have any effect on the budget negotiations at all," he said.
If the past is any guide, the one-day 500-point drop in 1987 did not inflict long-term harm on the economy, analysts said.
The stock market decline might push at least one issue further on the back burner -- privatisation of Social Security, which would allow those retirement funds to be invested in stocks.

"I bet you won't be hearing a whole lot about privatisation of Social Security in the next couple of weeks. This is one of the real arguments against privatising, who bears the risk of a downdraft in the market?" the Democrat congressional aide said.
If stock market declines persist, they could also act as one modest factor behind a push for a budget deal.
"One way to help the panicky financial markets is to reassure them by getting a budget deal, and so in a sense it supplies a modest, and I wouldn't want to oversell this, incentive," the aide said.
People on either side of the capital gains tax cut issue can use the stock market level to boost their argument.
Those opposed to a reduction in the tax on gains made from asset sales could say a capital gains tax cut when the stock market is falling might provide incentive for more selling.
"Will it (stock market decline) give a decided edge to one camp or the other, I don't think so," another congressional aide said.
